title: Can a grid with two odd sides ever be tiled?
description: A grid with m rows and n columns, where both m and n are odd. The number of squares is an odd number, and tiles always cover an even number of squares, so the grid can never be tiled. Keeko's doubt, that a bigger grid has more room, is struck.
teaching_notes: One idea: odd times odd is odd, and tiles cover only even numbers of squares. Watch for students who think a bigger grid helps.

source: Is an m × n grid tileable with 2 × 1 tiles if both m and n a
video_script.why: The child gives a reason that no grid with two odd sides can be tiled.
video_script.substitution: An odd number times an odd number is odd, and tiles cover only an even number of squares.
video_script.anchor: A grid of unit squares with m rows and n columns, where both m and n are odd, and a tile that covers 2 squares.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks a bigger odd grid might work, because it has more room. But more room does not change whether the count of squares is odd.
video_script.payoff_line: No, the grid cannot be tiled, because m times n is odd.

final_answer.value: No: m × n is odd, and tiles always cover an even number of squares
final_answer.spoken: no, because m times n is odd, and tiles always cover an even number of squares

hold_back: No: m × n is odd, and tiles always cover an even number of squares
maths_rules: The number of unit squares is m × n.
An odd number times an odd number is odd, for example 3 × 5 = 15.
Each tile covers 2 squares, so tiles always cover an even number of squares.
An odd number of squares can never be covered exactly.
Slip: a bigger odd grid still has an odd number of squares.
video_script.design: One general grid, then a check with three rows and five columns. The squares are paired off with one left over. The slip is thinking more room helps.
